More ranting
close

I see what you're getting at, but the way it's written here suggests that whatever is hiding behind that redaction is a component or components commonly used in buildings due to the nature of the other entries, and whatever it is, it can't be any worse than being able to destroy the earth itself if you point it down, which the article casually mentions later on. And since the materials the list does mention are all commonly used in buildings and bridges and other constructions of the sort the average reader assumes that whatever is behind that redaction is more of the same, and simply listing it along with the other common construction materials seems like it would do little harm.

Furthermore, if the redacted material was one commonly used in construction as the current state of the article suggests there would be little reason to redact it as the list already provides a fair amount of possible materials that can cause devastating results to both the Foundation and civilian life if destroyed that are not redacted, iron and steel being two prime examples and lord knows how many SCPs are contained in concrete chambers. If the redaction is to be kept in a similar style I feel it would be better off during the description of the contents of the "Other" tab, placing the redaction like so;

Selecting the "Other" option from the bottom of this list brings users to a different screen, enabling them to select other substances, including several types of wood, plastics, papers, [DATA EXPUNGED] and bone.

And while I'm aware this may come across as a bit grimdark it retains a sense of danger and the feel of the original redaction while not feeling out of place.

Either this or editing the other entries in the list somewhat to encompass a wider degree of materials than merely those commonly used in buildings would help the redaction feel a lot more like what's behind it is actually worthy of being redacted.

My point is, if there's anything that would fit behind the redaction as it is now that would simultaneously be not out of place and something actually redaction-worthy I can't think of it. Maybe it's just because I'm a big dum-dum, who knows?

Strongly disagree with this suggestion; the existing form is actually an example of how to do a throw-away [DATA EXPUNGED] correctly. No attention is drawn to it, and what was deleted is clearly telegraphed: a common construction material or materials.

 That aside, I think there's an aspect I think you're missing here:
In universe, it isn't notable, and they want to keep it that way.

Firstly, the Foundation and it's staff are fairly jaded to the anomalous; many redactions and expungements are for security reasons: things like not advertising how awesome of a weapon an SCP would make if someone were to steal it from containment locker 23 at site-██, or that if someone wanted to ruin the Foundation's day they should expose SCP-████ to SCP-████.

Second, note that it never says "material used for buildings". Just construction materials. Copper is a construction material. So is silicon. Aluminum, carbon fiber composites, porcelain and ceramic, crystalline minerals, and industrial/military grade alloys… all common construction materials. Attacking any of those could destroy a data center, annihilate a city's utility systems, cripple a modern attack tank… and if "living tissue" is behind that redaction, it's even worse.

item.content:encoded:
I like this. It's useful, but also a threat to the world at large if misused. The best kind of useful (in terms of SCP at least). I do wish to provide some criticism though.

Big rant wall of text below
Here it is

One small quibble: the description lists common construction materials SCP-219 lists in its menu, but then has a big [DATA EXPUNGED] all out of nowhere. What kind of material is common and non-anomalous enough to be a common construction material, but at the same time anomalous and secretive enough to be redacted from the description? I take it this material is anomalous or secret, possibly even another SCP, but then it shouldn't be listed in the same sentence as ordinary construction material. The way it is now, this redaction doesn't add anything to the article and just confuses readers. I'd like some clarification on this, recommending the following;

Using the keyboard, a user can select up to twenty items from a list of commonly used construction materials, including multiple varieties of stone, soil, bricks, concrete, steel, iron, [DATA EXPUNGED] and glass.

Be changed to this;

Using the keyboard, a user can select up to twenty items from a list of commonly used construction materials, including multiple varieties of stone, soil, bricks, concrete, steel, iron and glass. Notably, this list also includes [DATA EXPUNGED].

This way it is suggested that whoever made this device had knowledge of a material used exclusively in construction by a secretive organisation like the GOC or the Foundation and gives the redaction and by extension the article as a whole more weight to it. I realize this article is getting close to 7 years in age but I'm going to put this here anyway on the off chance the original author is still active on this site.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded: If this thing destroys every object of a given composition within a radius of at least 5 miles every time it's used, it's very implausible that people wouldn't have noticed. It'd be like having an SCP that exploded like a fusion bomb every time you used it - how does something like that go unnoticed before containment? Heck, it'd require a lot of effort to hide even the most subtle of tests (unless you set it for some esoteric custom-made material used solely for testing). This wide area of effect also makes the addendum about demolition use particularly absurd (I want to demolish this steel-framed building, so I'll use the machine that destroys all structural steel within at least five miles!).

item.content:encoded:
Re: 1 - Oh, is "media" the correct plural? I'll fix that up.

Re: 2 - Why is the minimum range of five miles a problem?

Re: 3 - I forgot about that. Editing article…

Re: 4 - I'm not sure, really. Looking over the other five Factory items in the SCP series, I don't see a definite pattern emerging among them. Yes, they're all small objects with bizarre functions, but besides that there's no real rhyme or reason as to whether they're benign or dangerous (or both). The only other thing they have in common is that they are all (apparently) man-made, and are exceptionally effective at their intended use. When I think of weird man-made objects that are more effective than they reasonably should be, mad scientist-types are what I think of first. Then again, this is a different kind of over-the-top item than the 110% stickers…

@Chubert: You're probably right. Removing bolded "History" text…

item.content:encoded:
1. I'd switch "mediums" for "media".

2. You've set the minimum range on this thing as 5 miles - so every time it's been tested it's destroyed everything of the chosen material(s) in at least a five-mile radius? Might want to tweak that…

3. Composition is not the only factor influencing resonant frequency. An object's size and shape also play key roles.

4. This doesn't seem suited to the Factory. Their stuff is generally more numerous, more innocuous-looking, and less physically plausible. This device feels more one-of-a-kind, the sort of thing you'd get from a mad scientist type. I defer, of course, to the judgment of those more senior than myself in such matters - this is just my take.
